item.title: The Effects of Search Interface on Consumer Preferences: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment
item.dc:creator: Jia Liu, Olivier Toubia
item.description:
Authors: Jia Liu, Olivier Toubia

DOI: 10.1287/mksc.2025.0261

Status: Articles in Advance / Online First

Online Publication Date: 2026-10-21

Abstract:
While structured search interfaces—such as filters and sorting tools—help consumers reduce search frictions on digital platforms, they also shape how consumers encounter product information during search. This paper studies how search interface design influences revealed preferences and market outcomes. We develop a theoretical framework linking interface design to attribute preferences through salience reallocation and information-based preference updating. The framework generates two predictions that can be formally derived: restricting faceted filters reduces the concentration of attribute importance weights (i.e., preference dispersion) and increases the diversity of products chosen (i.e., choice diversity). We test these predictions using a randomized, incentive-aligned online experiment in which 1,200 participants searched for wireless headphones on a custom-built e-commerce platform. Restricting filters led consumers to explore more broadly and resulted in more evenly distributed attribute importance weights and more diverse, higher-priced product choices. Mediation analysis further suggests that increased exploration was associated with shifts in attribute preferences. Our findings demonstrate that search interface design can construct, rather than merely reveal, consumer preferences.

item.title: The Motivational Paradox: How Aspirational-Goal Communications Influence Sales Performance and Information Acquisition
item.dc:creator: Doug J. Chung, Dongkyu Chang
item.description:
Authors: Doug J. Chung, Dongkyu Chang

DOI: 10.1287/mksc.2024.1051

Status: Articles in Advance / Online First

Online Publication Date: 2026-10-19

Abstract:
This study examines how aspirational-goal communications influence sales agents’ performance and information-seeking behavior. In a field experiment across 100 stores in Sweden, agents in the treatment group received daily personalized text messages with aspirational sales goals tailored to their prior performance. Results show that these communications increase sales performance, particularly among low-performing agents, primarily through higher unit sales. At the same time, they reduce agents’ willingness to monitor within-day sales progress—reflecting the ostrich effect—which can adversely affect performance. Information acquisition, in the form of sales-progress monitoring, typically aids effort provision, but aspirational-goal communications suppress such behavior, complicating performance management. These findings highlight the dual effects of aspirational-goal communications: while they enhance motivation, they may also prompt information avoidance. The study contributes to research on goal setting and sales management by clarifying the trade-offs in designing effective motivational and communication strategies.

item.title: AI in Disguise—Quasi-Experimental Analysis of a Large-Scale Deployment of AI-Generated Ads
item.dc:creator: Yannick Exner, Jochen Hartmann, Ziqian Ding, Shunyuan Zhang, Oded Netzer
item.description:
Authors: Yannick Exner, Jochen Hartmann, Ziqian Ding, Shunyuan Zhang, Oded Netzer

DOI: 10.1287/mksc.2025.0547

Status: Articles in Advance / Online First

Online Publication Date: 2026-10-19

Abstract:
As Taboola prepared to launch its GenAI Ad Maker, a tool that lets advertisers create ad images within the platform, it faced a consequential question about whether AI-generated ad images would perform well with real consumers, and under what conditions. Working with Taboola, we construct a quasi-experimental comparison of 4,633 ‘sibling ads,’ meaning AI-generated and human-made images launched by the same advertisers, in identical campaign settings, at the same time. These ads span more than 369 million impressions and 2.5 million clicks. We do not find a detectable average click-through-rate disadvantage for AI-generated images relative to their human-made siblings. However, this average masks an important boundary condition: ads with AI-generated images outperform human-made ads when the AI images do not ‘look like AI.’ We identify key visual features influencing consumers’ perceptions of whether an ad looks AI-generated. While AI generates sharper, clearer, and less blurry images with larger faces, consumers associate these features with human-made ads. On the other hand, in line with consumers’ expectations, aesthetics, lower warmth, and intense color saturation in ads signal AI generation. These findings support Taboola’s roll-out communication, advertiser guidance, and continued refinement of the GenAI Ad Maker.

item.title: Music Marketing with Generative AI
item.dc:creator: Benedikt Roder, Jochen Hartmann
item.description:
Authors: Benedikt Roder, Jochen Hartmann

DOI: 10.1287/mksc.2025.0150

Status: Articles in Advance / Online First

Online Publication Date: 2026-10-14

Abstract:
The multibillion-dollar music industry faces severe content creation bottlenecks, making multimedia marketing assets prohibitively costly for smaller artists. This practice paper introduces a Marketing Asset Generation Engine (MAGE) that can produce over 700 million video ad variations reflecting each artist’s visual identity using only a music track’s audio and album cover as inputs. Collaborating with one of the world’s largest music labels, we conduct four preregistered field studies with over 11 million impressions across 75 campaigns for 33 music tracks on TikTok and Meta to validate MAGE. First, pooled across studies, MAGE-generated ads significantly outperform human-designed ads on TikTok with on average 26% higher click-through rates and 10% higher engagement, while we do not detect statistically significant performance differences on Meta, all at 98% lower production cost. Second, neither marketing professionals nor laypeople can reliably identify winning ads such that random sampling of MAGE’s outputs performs as well as human-curated selections. In contrast, an AI-in-the-loop system trained on past performance data can predict pre-launch which MAGE-generated ads will perform best for specific audience segments. These findings demonstrate that generative AI democratizes music marketing by making effective, on-brand video ads accessible at scale.

item.title: The Identification of the Dynamic Discrete-Choice Model with Stockpiling
item.dc:creator: Xinyao Kong, Jean-Pierre Dubé, Vaness Alwan
item.description:
Authors: Xinyao Kong, Jean-Pierre Dubé, Vaness Alwan

DOI: 10.1287/mksc.2024.1280

Status: Articles in Advance / Online First

Online Publication Date: 2026-10-08

Abstract:
We study the identification of the discount factor for dynamic discrete-choice (DDC) models of demand with stockpiling of a storable good. We show that the DDC has built-in exclusion restrictions that set-identify the discount factor without requiring any auxiliary assumptions. We compare this approach to previous work that assumes auxiliary structure on the storage cost function, clarifying how such structure generates exclusion restrictions and the corresponding data moments used for identification. Our key results show that these auxiliary restrictions are not necessary for identification; but that they are testable and can be included to achieve point identification and improve statistical efficiency. Using a case study of laundry detergent from earlier published work, we find a mean discount factor estimate of $0.957$, rejecting myopic models of choice in favor of the dynamic model. In counterfactual simulations, we show that some of the promotional lift during a discount period is indeed due to forward-buying. However, we predict considerably higher incremental sales compared to a standard discrete-choice model, which predicts that promotional discounts mainly cause substitution between brands. These results contribute to the long-standing discussion about the effectiveness of price promotions.

item.title: Brand-Neutral Content Marketing and Endogenous Search Prominence
item.dc:creator: Michelle Y. Lu
item.description:
Authors: Michelle Y. Lu

DOI: 10.1287/mksc.2023.0558

Status: Articles in Advance / Online First

Online Publication Date: 2026-09-30

Abstract:
Brand-neutral content marketing attracts consumers by addressing category-level needs without directly promoting the brand. Although this may position a firm as consumers’ first point of inquiry, it leaves consumers only partially informed about brand fit. Rivals can exploit this gap by providing brand-specific information. Using a game-theoretic framework, we examine when content marketing generates endogenous search prominence and how the resulting search dynamics shape competitive communication strategies. We show that content marketing can provide a counterintuitive competitive edge: by shaping the information structure of consumer search, it influences rival pricing incentives, giving rise to asymmetric communication equilibria sustained by an information–exploitation tradeoff that governs profit allocation between the prominent gatekeeper and the non-prominent follower. When prices cannot be credibly committed, exploitation permanently dominates and content marketing becomes the unique equilibrium strategy. Brand strength and appeal breadth further determine which firm adopts content marketing.

item.title: Algorithmic Targeting and the Precision-Recall Tradeoff
item.dc:creator: Ganesh Iyer, Yunfei (Jesse) Yao, Zemin (Zachary) Zhong
item.description:
Authors: Ganesh Iyer, Yunfei (Jesse) Yao, Zemin (Zachary) Zhong

DOI: 10.1287/mksc.2024.0930

Status: Volume 45, Issue 4

Online Publication Date: 2026-07-01

Abstract:
We examine the implications of competitive algorithmic targeting when outcomes of targeting algorithms are the individual consumer-level predicted probabilities of conversion. In these situations, firms implicitly face the well-known precision-recall tradeoff while choosing their targeting strategies. They can choose to target a smaller set of consumers with a high probability of conversion (precision) but miss out on many consumers who might still be interested in their product. Conversely, firms can target a larger set of consumers (recall), but this results in a greater probability that their targeting is wasted on uninterested consumers. We analyze this precision-recall tradeoff under competition between firms that strategically choose their algorithmic targeting policies. We show that competing firms favor a targeting policy that has higher precision but lower recall compared with a monopoly. Firms target fewer consumers when their algorithms are more correlated. They also have the incentive to strategically decrease the precision of their targeting policies in order to reduce competition. If firms endogenously choose their algorithmic correlation, then there is an equilibrium incentive to decrease the correlation. History: Anthony Dukes served as the senior editor for this article. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2024.0930 .
